Introduction/Tech Scan

Development guide

Tech Scan

Tech Scan maps each concept in this guide to the products that implement it, with an AWS-first default and a conditional alternative where one exists. It is a product map, not a vendor endorsement and not a buying guide.

This section is a draft. It publishes the hub and four spokes first — Models, Harness, AI gateway and Sandbox — and adds the remaining spokes in later waves. Entries are research references from web sources reviewed 11–12 November 2026, not locally deployed or benchmarked options. Publishing a clearly labelled research reference does not mean the infrastructure has passed its qualification tests. [2]

Read the matching Concepts section before choosing a product. Tech Scan answers which product implements a concept; it does not re-explain the concept. Cloud scope is AWS only: no other cloud platform is named as an option. The model policy is managed Claude or OpenAI models, with Amazon Bedrock preferred; direct provider APIs are exceptions. [1]

Purpose and scope

Concepts explains what the playbook's ideas are: intent, specification, context, harness, loop, graph, software factories and model selection. It names a few tools, but a team choosing a stack still has to map each concept to a concrete product. Tech Scan is that map. [1]

Use it when the team has agreed what it needs and must choose what implements it. Start from the concept, follow its link to the spoke, and compare the default with the alternative trigger before adopting either. A product that cannot name the concept it implements does not belong in Tech Scan.

Tech Scan is a reference section, not a lifecycle stage. It does not change the lifecycle, and it does not rewrite Concepts into an AWS product manual. Each spoke links back to the Concepts section it implements. [1]

What Tech Scan does not do

  • Recommend a vendor. An AWS-first default is a starting point for a team on AWS, not an endorsement. A conditional alternative is offered only with its trigger.
  • Compare prices. Prices move monthly; verify them on the vendor page when the decision is made. No prices appear in Tech Scan.
  • Prove a product works here. No option in Tech Scan has been locally deployed or benchmarked. A public customer case does not establish this team's performance or compliance. [1]
  • Cover every product. One default and at most one justified alternative appear per capability. Further candidates stay in optional detail on the spoke, not in a second parallel stack.

How to read an entry

Every spoke follows the same shape, so a reader can compare entries without relearning the layout. The spoke states its purpose and the Concepts section it implements, then gives the AWS-first default, the conditional alternative with its trigger, research-only notes, a list of products not to use, and the gaps that remain. [2]

How to read a Tech Scan entry
LabelWhat it means
AWS-first defaultThe starting point for a team on AWS. It must still pass the hard gates:
  • Required capability
  • Approved data location and retention
  • Identity and authorisation
  • Supported model and API
  • Security boundaries
  • Operational ownership
Conditional alternativeUse it only when its stated trigger applies, such as a capability the default cannot express. Compatibility claims alone do not qualify an alternative.
Research-only noteInteresting, not recommended. Read it to understand the option, not to adopt it.
Do not useRetired, archived, shut down or superseded. This list matters as much as the recommendations: products in it are still named in older guides.

Each entry also carries its evidence label. The labels are vendor availability claim, public customer-reported operation, AWS or vendor reference deployment and locally validated. No Tech Scan entry is locally validated. Keep the labels distinct: a customer case, a reference deployment and a local test are different kinds of evidence. [1]

Status words on a product mean what the vendor states: GA means generally available, Preview means not yet generally available. A product's status can change quickly — several products named in 2026 research shut down or were archived within months — so every spoke records the status it relied on and the spoke's own review date. [2]

Wave 1: Models, Harness, Gateway, Sandbox

Wave 1 publishes the four spokes whose material was already researched in November 2026. Each spoke can move from draft to stable on its own; the table records its status, so one slow spoke never blocks the rest. The Sandbox spoke's default, AWS Nitro Sandboxes, launched 9 November 2026.[3] The Harness spoke's default is the config-based, Strands-powered managed harness.[4] [2]

Cross-cutting views

Two views cut across every layer, so they are not layers themselves. The AWS platform view covers the AWS services as a whole: the service map across layers, Singapore availability, GA versus preview status, retired services to avoid, and the account, identity and network guardrails that apply everywhere. The language view shows what the playbook's gates look like in each stack — Java, TypeScript with React, Python — and links to the layer rows instead of copying them. React is a framework, not a language, and the languages page says so. [2]

One rule keeps the section scalable: each product row lives on exactly one spoke. Language pages and the AWS platform link to it; they never copy it. A product that is archived or renamed is corrected in one place. [2]

The shared integration standards are the same on every spoke:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) for tools and documentation.
  • OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics and logs.
  • Spec Kit with OKF (the Open Knowledge Format, a Markdown format) for specifications and standards.
  • GitLab or GitHub as the source of truth for issues and merge requests.
  • SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) or JSON for scanner findings.

A spoke that needs a standard states which one; a product that breaks a standard is a worse fit, even when it is the default. [1]

Gaps stated plainly

No layer forces single-vendor lock-in, but AWS has no managed equivalent for several needs. The gaps below apply across spokes; each spoke repeats only the gaps that affect its own entries. [1]

  • Issue tracking. AWS has no managed issue tracker in this stack. The tracker stays in GitHub or GitLab, and AWS-first does not require repository migration.
  • Dynamic testing. AWS Security Agent on-demand penetration testing is generally available, while its documented CI/CD integration remains in preview. It is a managed dynamic-security option, not a one-for-one replacement for repeatable OWASP ZAP checks. Authorised pre-production scope, credentials, bounded waits and fail-closed behaviour are required before adoption.
  • Threat modelling, DORA measurement, mutation and architecture testing. No AWS managed service covers these. They run as self-hosted tools on the team's own infrastructure even in the AWS stack.
  • Typed decisions: Box. A typed decision is an answer a model returns in a fixed form the team can check mechanically, such as a choice, a score, a yes/no question or a visual grounding box. The remaining gap is specifically Box, visual grounding as a typed decision; see Tech Scan: Models for the four types. No open-weight rival has been verified to document it, and the Decider evaluation stopped before its local test, so Decider is not adopted and its reported numbers are not settled.
  • Policy packs. The Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) and Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC) policy packs are harness content, not a product. The gap on both stacks is encoding the machine-verifiable controls as checks and protecting guardrail files, then retaining reviewed evidence and manual approval for the remainder.

Where each layer lives

The original proposal listed ten technology layers. Every layer maps to a spoke below, or to an explicit exclusion. Nothing is silently dropped. [1]

LayerWhere it lives
1. LLM and model hostingModels (Wave 1). Self-hosted inference is excluded from the recommended route by the model policy.
2. Agent harness and orchestrationHarness (Wave 1).
3. Context engineering and retrievalContext spoke (Wave 3, planned).
4. Task specification and work trackingWorkflows spoke (Wave 2, planned).
5. Execution environment and sandboxSandbox (Wave 1).
6. Verification in the build loopVerification spoke (Wave 3, planned).
7. Quality gates and ProductOps Quality ModelVerification spoke (Wave 3, planned).

9. Security, governance and policy as codeDelivery spoke (Wave 3, planned).

Next step: Choose the question you need answered and open its spoke. Start with Models when the choice is which model runs the work, or Sandbox when untrusted agent code needs somewhere safe to run.
